title: Writing for governors, 1428–30
dramatic_question: Three readers are named in the works of these years: a Ḥanbalī named ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn b. Bāysunghur, a man named Shāh Rażī l-Dīn, at whose request you wrote, and your own son. In exile your writing is also your credit. For whom do you write first, and in what register?

invariants.text: The Tuḥfa-yi ʿAlāʾī, a brief treatment of the hadith on iḥsān, īmān and islām, was completed on 1 Jumādā I 831/17 February 1428 for ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn b. Bāysunghur, a Ḥanbalī.
invariants.detail: Melvin-Koushki prints the date without an asterisk and does not name its source.

invariants.text: The Mabdaʾ u Maʿād was written at the request of one Shāh Rażī l-Dīn and completed early Ṣafar 832/mid-November 1428 at Manzil-i Chālū in Mazandaran, the same date and place as its Majlis 10196 copy.
The K. al-Manāhij, on logic, was written for his son Muḥammad and completed at Natanz on 20 Rajab 833/14 April 1430, the same day and place as its Majlis 10196 copy.

prose: Exile has not stopped your pen. Three works from these years carry dates, each for a different reader. The dates are Melvin-Koushki's: in the later part of MS Majlis 10196 he takes them to approximate composition, and the Tuḥfa's has no named source.

The Tuḥfa-yi ʿAlāʾī, for ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn b. Bāysunghur, a Ḥanbalī, takes the hadith on iḥsān, īmān and islām through the five fundamentals of practice and looks at how Ḥanbalīs and Shāfiʿīs each perform them. The Mabdaʾ u Maʿād gives Shāh Rażī l-Dīn, at his request, an overview of the religious sciences in the mystical manner. The Manāhij is a minutely detailed treatise on logic, in the manner of the latter-day philosophers, for Muḥammad.
You cannot write all three at once. Which do you take up first?

choices.label: Take up the Tuḥfa-yi ʿAlāʾī first, for ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn b. Bāysunghur, and the other two commissions after it.
choices.feedback: This is the order Melvin-Koushki's dates give: February 1428, November 1428, April 1430. In the Tuḥfa you say your family has always been Shāfiʿī, and its introduction complains of the harsh treatment you had in Herat; those are statements to a patron, so they show what you told ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn, not clearly what you held. The game credits no standing with him, since no page read identifies him beyond his name, and only a small one with Shāh Rażī l-Dīn, whose request is recorded but not what he did for you.

choices.label: Take up the K. al-Manāhij first, for your son Muḥammad, so he has his logic before any patron is asked.
choices.feedback: You did write the Manāhij for Muḥammad, but at Natanz in April 1430, after the other two; the sources do not have it first. This is your own what-if, and the game returns you to the record: all three works are dated, and the patrons' works come first. What you gained and paid here stays in your ledger; the story then rejoins the record.
costs: Your son is taught and the manual circulates. No patron is served first, so no stipend comes yet.

choices.label: Take up a new lettrist treatise first, for Bāysunghur, and ask him for his help instead of the commissions.
costs: A prince who favoured you may help with your household. Lettrist writing is what your enemies read as Ḥurūfī sympathy, and exposure rises.
choices.feedback: Open to you because Bāysunghur has favoured you: he received you with particular favour and asked for the R. Suʾl al-Mulūk. The sources show no lettrist work for him from the exile; the one thing you address to him in these years is the second apology, later. The Iṣbāḥ al-Anwār, your fuller lettrist work, is the one Melvin-Koushki conjectures you left unfinished after 1427. The game returns you to the record. What you gained and paid here stays in your ledger; the story then rejoins the record.
